units.text:
Control Charts for Attributes
Definition of Attribute Data and Examples
Attribute data refers to quality characteristics that are counted or classified
rather than measured on a continuous scale. An attribute describes something
in terms of distinct categories or labels, usually as "conforming" (meets a
standard) or "nonconforming" (fails to meet a standard). In statistics and
quality control, attribute data is measured on a nominal scale—for example,
pass/fail, accept/reject, or by counting the number of occurrences of a specific
event.
Examples:
• Counting the number of faulty (nonconforming) light bulbs in a batch.
•  Recording if a product passes or fails a final inspection.
•  Tallying the number of errors or defects on a printed page.
•  Classifying a food item as "acceptable" or "not acceptable" based on taste.
•  Recording the number of insurance claims filed due to errors in policy
  processing.

Importance of Attribute Control Charts:


   • Attribute control charts provide a cost-effective and simple
    method for monitoring processes where direct measurement is
     impractical or unnecessary.
   • They help in summarizing overall quality at various
     organizational levels (e.g., operator, department, plant).
   • Useful when decisions are based on compliance with
     specifications rather than degree of conformance.

units.text:
Application of Attribute Control Charts in Quality
Control

Key Applications:
•  Manufacturing: Monitoring the proportion of defective parts,
   tracking the number of flaws in batches, or counting faulty units.
•  Service industry: Recording customer complaints, transaction
   errors, or incorrect billing instances.
•  Healthcare: Counting adverse events (e.g., infections, medication
   errors) or monitoring mortality/morbidity rates.
•  Logistics: Proportion of on-time deliveries versus late deliveries.
•  Administrative processes: Counting the number of application
   rejections, claims processed incorrectly, or forms returned for
   corrections.

units.text:
Why Use Attribute Charts?

•  They allow for overall assessment of process quality, especially when
  measuring every output dimension is impractical.
•  They are straightforward for operators to understand and
  implement.
•  Suitable for high-volume processes or when quick, binary (pass/fail)
  feedback is essential.
•  Examples include p-charts (proportion nonconforming), np-charts
  (number nonconforming), c-charts (number of nonconformities),
  and u-charts (nonconformities per unit).
By deploying attribute control charts, organizations can efficiently
monitor, identify, and address quality issues, thereby supporting
ongoing process improvement and customer satisfaction.

Advantages of Attribute Control Charts

• Simplicity of Use: Attribute charts are easy to construct and interpret, making them
  accessible for operators and managers at all organizational levels.
• Summarization: They allow you to condense multiple quality characteristics or
  components into a single, overall quality indicator. For example, a product that must
  meet specifications for length, width, and height can be monitored with one
  attribute chart instead of three variable charts.
• Cost and Resource Efficiency: Ideal for cases where measuring each characteristic as
  a variable is too expensive, time-consuming, or resource-intensive. Attribute data
  collection often requires less specialized equipment—sometimes just a visual
  inspection or a go/no-go gage.
• Broad Applicability: Can be used for summarizing quality at higher organizational
  levels (e.g., plant, department, company), helping to quickly identify where
  problems are occurring without the need to track every individual process
  parameter.
• Suitable for Certain Quality Characteristics: Some quality characteristics (e.g., taste,
  visual appearance, presence of a scratch) are inherently categorical and can’t be
  meaningfully measured as variables

units.text:
Disadvantages of Attribute Control Charts

• Lack of Detailed Information: Attribute charts provide only "conforming" or
  "nonconforming" data—they do not indicate by how much a measurement
  deviates from the target. This means they do not show the degree of
  variability or how close items are to specification limits.
• Limited Diagnostic Power: They do not provide insights into the mean or the
  spread of the distribution, so it’s harder to diagnose the root cause of
  process shifts compared to variable charts (like X̄ and R charts).
• Slower Detection: Attribute charts may not signal a process shift until out-
  of-spec items actually occur. Variable charts can sometimes warn of
  impending problems before any defectives are produced.
• Require Larger Sample Sizes: To achieve the same sensitivity as variable
  charts, attribute charts often require larger samples—especially problematic
 when inspection is costly or destructive.

Chart for Number of Nonconformities: c-Chart

A nonconformity is defined as a quality characteristic that does not meet
some specification. A nonconforming item has one or more
nonconformities that make it nonfunctional. It is also possible for a
product to have one or more nonconformities and still conform to
standards. The p- and np-charts deal with nonconforming items. A c-
chart is used to track the total number of nonconformities in samples of
constant size. When the sample size varies, a u-chart is used to track the
number of nonconformities per unit. In constructing c- and u-charts, the
size of the sample is also referred to as the area of opportunity.
The occurrence of nonconformities is assumed to follow a Poisson
distribution. If x represents the number of nonconformities in the
sample unit and c is the mean, then the Poisson distribution yields

units.text:
Chart for Number of Nonconformities Per Unit: u-
Chart

A c-chart is used when the sample size is constant. If the area of
 opportunity changes from one sample to another, the centerline and
 control limits of a c-chart change as well. For situations in which the
sample size varies, a u-chart is used. For companies that inspect all
 items produced or services rendered for the presence of
 nonconformities, the output per production run can vary because of
 fluctuating supplies of labor, machinery, and raw material;
 consequently, the number inspected per production run changes,
 thus causing varying sample sizes. When the sample size varies, a u-
 chart is constructed to monitor the number of nonconformities per
 unit. Even though the control limits change as the sample size varies,
 the centerline of a u-chart remains constant, which permits
 meaningful comparisons between the samples.

units.text:
Chart for Demerits Per Unit: U-Chart

The regular c- and u-charts treat all types of nonconformities equally
 regardless of their degree of severity. Let’s suppose that in inspecting
computer monitors we find that one monitor has trouble retaining
 consistent color and a second monitor has five scratch marks on its
 surface. Using either a c- or u-chart, the relative importance of
 monitor 2’s defects, in terms of the number of nonconformities, is
 five times as great as that of monitor 1. However, the single defect
 associated with monitor 1 is much more serious than monitor 2’s
 scratch marks. An alternative approach assigns weights to
 nonconformities according to their relative degree of severity. This
 quality rating system, which rates demerits per unit and is called the
 U-chart, thus overcomes the deficiency of the c- and u-charts. These
 are often helpful in service applications.

Use of Geometric Distribution for Discrete Variables:
For a highly conforming process, non conforming items are few and far
between. This implies that monitoring the number of nonconforming
items will yield most observations with values of zero, which prevents
the detection of a change in the nonconformance rate. An alternative is
to monitor the number of items until a nonconforming item is found,
sometimes referred to as the number of trials upto the first success (X).
When a nonconforming item is found, the count starts a new. The
